# Where this session starts

## What session 02 handed over

A discharge you can place in time --- when it broke down, what the coils did,
and a vacuum field you have checked against the magnetics.

This session asks what the plasma settled *into*, how anyone knows, and how
well the stored answer explains what was measured.

::: {.notes}
[2 min]

NARRATE:
Name the prerequisite. Session 02 ended with a field and a breakdown time;
session 03 begins after the current has ramped and the plasma has found a shape.

The session's posture is unusual and worth flagging early: it does not take the
reconstruction on trust. It asks what the reconstruction was given, how much
each input was trusted, and whether the stored equilibrium satisfies its own
governing equation.

TRANSITION:
The whole session is one chain, and it is worth putting on the screen.
:::

## The chain

shape $\rightarrow$ force-balanced analytic equilibrium $\rightarrow$
experimental reconstruction $\rightarrow$ validation $\rightarrow$
flux coordinates $\rightarrow$ kinetic profiles $\rightarrow$
derived plasma state $\rightarrow$ self-consistency

::: {.notes}
[1 min]

NARRATE:
Point at each arrow. Every arrow is a place where a model or an assumption
enters, and the session stops at each one to say which. The notebook's steps
follow the arrows in order.
:::

# The equation

## The equation everything rests on

$$\nabla p = \mathbf{J}\times\mathbf{B}
\;\;\Longrightarrow\;\;
\Delta^{*}\psi = -\mu_{0}R^{2}p'(\psi) - FF'(\psi)$$

Axisymmetric, static, isotropic pressure, nested surfaces.

::: {.notes}
[5 min]

NARRATE:
Read the equation as a statement about force balance collapsing, under
axisymmetry, to one scalar equation for $\psi$. Everything else follows from
$\psi$: the surfaces are its contours, the field is its gradient.

Two free functions, $p'$ and $FF'$. That is what makes reconstruction possible
and also what makes it under-determined.

Say the four assumptions out loud, and where each fails: strong rotation,
pressure anisotropy, 3-D fields, islands and stochastic regions. Those are
session 05; this session assumes the standard form throughout.

WARN:
Background the course never defines and this session then uses. Supply it here:

- **last closed flux surface** — the outermost surface whose field lines close
  on themselves; outside it they strike a wall. On a *diverted* plasma that
  surface passes through an X-point and is called a **separatrix**; VEST
  discharges are mostly limited on the centre stack, so the boundary is set by
  the limiter instead. The notebook's Solov'ev examples show all three
  topologies side by side.
- **$q$** and **$q_{95}$** — $q$ is the field-line pitch, toroidal turns per
  poloidal turn; $q_{95}$ is its value at 95% of the normalised poloidal flux.
  The convention exists because $q$ diverges at an X-point, so an edge value
  quoted *at* the boundary is unusable on a diverted plasma; it is quoted the
  same way on limited ones so the number stays comparable between machines.
- **$\beta$** — plasma pressure over magnetic pressure. Toroidal, poloidal and
  normalised betas are different numbers.
- **$\ell_i$** — internal inductance, how peaked the current profile is.

TRANSITION:
Before a real discharge, the vocabulary: what an equilibrium is made of.
:::

# Representing an equilibrium

## A hierarchy, not a boundary

- **2-D** --- $\psi(R,Z)$, fields, LCFS, axis, X-points, wall
- **1-D** --- $q$, $p$, $F$, $p'$, $FF'$
- **global** --- $I_p$, $a$, $\kappa$, $\delta$, $q_{95}$, $\beta_N$, $\ell_i$
- **coordinates** --- $\psi_N$, $\rho_{\mathrm{tor},N}$, $R$, $r$

::: {.notes}
[3 min]

NARRATE:
The four levels, and which one the solver actually solves for: the 1-D source
functions. The 2-D map follows from them; the global numbers summarise them.

WARN:
The packaged 39915 slices store a `rho_tor_norm` that is exactly
$\sqrt{\psi_N}$ --- a proxy. The notebook checks it before and after
derivation. Make the point that a coordinate's *name* in a file is not proof of
what it is.
:::

## A shape is not a solution

**Miller** --- five numbers per surface, any nesting.

**Solov'ev** --- constant $p'$, $FF'$: every surface follows.

**Guazzotto--Freidberg** --- smooth sources; $\kappa$, $\delta$, $\nu \approx \beta_p$ in,
axis, $\beta_p$, $\ell_i$, $q_{95}$ out.

Limited, single null, double null: a property of the flux map.

::: {.notes}
[4 min]

NARRATE:
Miller is how a gyrokinetic or stability code describes a local surface
*given* an equilibrium. It carries no force balance. Solov'ev is an exact
solution of the Grad--Shafranov equation, rich enough (Cerfon--Freidberg) to
impose a boundary and an X-point. Guazzotto--Freidberg makes the sources
vanish at the edge and has a pressure knob, $\nu$. The notebook scans
$\kappa$, $\delta$ and $\nu$ at the shape of the discharge: every panel title
is a response, and none of them is $\ell_i$ as an input.

Topology is decided from the saddles of $\psi$: a saddle whose flux matches the
boundary's makes the plasma diverted. Real VEST maps have many saddles, far
outside the plasma; none of them is on the boundary.
:::

## Inputs and responses

| input | responses |
| --- | --- |
| $\kappa$ | shape, axis, $\beta_p$, $\ell_i$, $q_{95}$ |
| $\delta$ | shape, axis, $\beta_p$, $\ell_i$, $q_{95}$ |
| $\nu \approx \beta_p$ | pressure, Shafranov shift, $\ell_i$, $q_{95}$ |

There is no $\ell_i$ knob.

::: {.notes}
[5 min]

NARRATE:
The Guazzotto--Freidberg model at the shape of the discharge, one input turned
at a time. Raising $\nu$ moves the axis outward: the Shafranov shift. Raising
$\kappa$ raises $q_{95}$ and lowers $\ell_i$, a geometric effect because the
source profile is fixed. Then the model at the discharge's own shape and
$\beta_p$ against EFIT: the axis agrees within millimetres, $\ell_i$ does not,
because the model fixes the current-profile shape and EFIT fitted its own.

TRANSITION:
In the experiment nobody hands you $\nu$. The next slides are optional depth on
the equation itself (deep dive A in the notebook); skip to the constraints if
time is short.
:::

## One flux function, three regions

$$\Delta^*\psi = -\mu_0 R J_\phi \quad\text{everywhere}$$

| region | equation |
| --- | --- |
| plasma | $\Delta^*\psi = -\mu_0R^2p'(\psi) - FF'(\psi)$ |
| vacuum | $\Delta^*\psi = 0$ (homogeneous) |
| coils, vessel | $\Delta^*\psi = -\mu_0 R J_{\phi,\mathrm{ext}}$ |

$\psi = \psi_{\mathrm{plasma}} + \psi_{\mathrm{coil}} + \psi_{\mathrm{passive}}$: same flux, different sources.

::: {.notes}
[4 min]

NARRATE:
Ampère's law is the common start; force balance is what adds physics inside
the plasma, by forcing the current to be built from two flux functions. In the
vacuum the equation is source-free. The notebook builds a flux map from a
plasma and two coil pairs and checks both region equations on it.

TRANSITION:
Where does the plasma end? That depends on who is asked to decide.
:::

## The boundary: input or output

- **fixed boundary**: $\psi|_{\partial\Omega_p} = \psi_b$ --- the boundary is an input
- **free boundary**: coils and sources given --- the boundary is **part of the solution**
- LCFS = separatrix through an X-point ($\nabla\psi = 0$), or the last closed surface touching the limiter
- same plasma, add a shaping coil pair: two X-points appear, the topology changes

::: {.notes}
[4 min]

NARRATE:
Name the magnetic axis, the separatrix, the scrape-off layer and the private
flux region on the notebook's figure. Stress that the example is a
superposition with the current held fixed: its axis does not sit where the
current is centred, and removing that mismatch is what a free-boundary solver
iterates for.

TRANSITION:
Which is why the problem class has two axes.
:::

## Two axes of numerical problems

|                | fixed boundary | free boundary        |
|----------------|----------------|----------------------|
| forward        | CHEASE         | TES, TokaMaker       |
| reconstruction | ---            | EFIT                 |

Free-boundary and inverse are **not** synonyms. DCON, RDCON, GPEC sit outside
the table: they take any of these equilibria as input.

::: {.notes}
[3 min]

NARRATE:
The distinction students most often blur. EFIT is given measurements and finds
the equilibrium most consistent with them; its answer is only as good as the
diagnostics constrain it. CHEASE is given a boundary and two profiles and solves
to numerical precision; it cannot tell you about a discharge it was not given.

Free versus fixed boundary is the concrete difference: EFIT's grid extends past
the plasma to the coils because the boundary is part of the answer. CHEASE works
only inside a boundary you hand it.

TRANSITION:
So what was EFIT actually given?
:::

# What the experiment constrains

## Measured, weighted, reconstructed

$$r_i = \frac{y_i - y_i^{\mathrm{model}}}{\sigma_i}$$

Only as meaningful as $\sigma_i$.

::: {.notes}
[5 min]

NARRATE:
The inputs: plasma current, PF currents, poloidal probes, flux loops,
diamagnetic flux --- measured; vessel currents --- modelled; the limiter ---
geometry.

Then the honest part, which the notebook prints rather than asserts. On these
samples EFIT reports an $I_p$ $\chi^2$ of about 200 although the reconstructed
$I_p$ equals the measured one to float precision: all of it is the vessel term
of a Rogowski that encloses the vessel, and VEST's inner Rogowski does not
(#918). VAFT recomputes the plasma-only residual, which is essentially zero.
What remains is dominated by the probes and is tiny, because EFIT's $\sigma$ is its
weight times $10^4$: about 1000 T for a probe, while the diagnostic recorded
1%. The ratio is of order $10^6$. The weights, not the diagnostics, set the
fit. And the diamagnetic loop was submitted as $|\Delta\Phi|$ at weight
$10^{-4}$, so it did not constrain the pressure.

WARN:
Do not let this turn into "EFIT is wrong". The flux map can be fine. What
cannot be used is the stored $\chi^2$ as evidence of fit quality.
:::

## Four layers

**Measured** $\rightarrow$ **reconstructed / fitted** $\leftarrow$ **assumed / prior**

$\downarrow$

**Derived**

::: {.notes}
[2 min]

NARRATE:
The provenance diagram of step 5 is the reference for the rest of the session.
A probe signal is measured; $\psi(R,Z)$ is reconstructed; EFIT's weights and a
chosen $Z_\mathrm{eff}$ are assumed; $\beta_N$ is derived. Some assumptions
enter only the derivation. A derived number is never itself a measurement.
:::

## The coordinate is borrowed

$(R_i, Z_i) \rightarrow \psi_{N,i} \rightarrow \rho_{\mathrm{tor},N,i}$

The measurement does not move; its radius does.

::: {.notes}
[4 min]

NARRATE:
Thomson and charge-exchange channels mapped through a magnetic and a kinetic
EFIT of the same instant land at different $\rho$. Then the fits: judged by
$\chi^2_\nu$ with $\nu$ and $k$ stated, not by eye.

Three moments worth pausing on in the notebook: five Thomson points leave two
degrees of freedom; a Gaussian process on five points collapses to a constant;
the charge-exchange chord crosses the magnetic axis and its two sides disagree,
which is a question about the equilibrium's axis as much as about the ions.

WARN:
$Z_{\mathrm{eff}}$ is composition information, not another profile point, and
VAFT has no visible-bremsstrahlung $Z_{\mathrm{eff}}$ workflow yet. On VEST it
is an assumption you state.
:::

# What is stored, and what is not

## What a g-file does not carry

Six profiles are stored. Volume, shape, $\beta$ and $\ell_i$ are **derived**.

A refused plot is often an underived quantity, not a missing measurement.

::: {.notes}
[3 min]

NARRATE:
This is the session's transferable habit, and it recurs in session 04 inverted.
A g-file is a compact format: $\psi$ on a grid plus six one-dimensional
profiles. Everything else a physicist quotes about an equilibrium is computed
from those.

So when VAFT refuses to plot $\beta_N$, the question to ask is not "does this
shot lack it" but "has anything derived it yet".

WARN:
Conventions bite here. $\beta_p$ names three different quantities in common use,
differing by up to 26% at VEST's aspect ratio, and $\ell_i$ has at least three
definitions. VAFT states which it computes; a number quoted without its
convention is not a number.

TRANSITION:
Which brings up the convention that governs all of this.
:::

## The convention you will meet next

VAFT works internally in **COCOS 11** --- the convention the IMAS Data
Dictionary mandates.

Poloidal flux in full weber, not weber per radian.

::: {.notes}
[3 min]

NARRATE:
COCOS is not mentioned anywhere in this course's notebooks, and it is the first
thing that will confuse a reader who leaves the tutorial for the library. Spend
three minutes.

Sixteen conventions exist [@sauter2013cocos]. They differ in the orientation of
the toroidal and poloidal coordinates, the sign of the poloidal flux, and
whether that flux is divided by $2\pi$. Equilibrium quantities are only
comparable between codes once the index is known.

The practical consequence for this course: EFIT g-files are usually COCOS 1–8,
which store $\psi$ per radian; the Data Dictionary and VAFT's Green's functions
use full weber. A factor of $2\pi$ between them is the single most common
equilibrium bug --- the notebook's flux-loop table carries exactly that $2\pi$.

WARN:
Do not tell students to "just multiply by $2\pi$". The conversion carries both
the $2\pi$ and an orientation sign, and applying only the first leaves the field
inverted for half the indices. The packaged CHEASE g-file declares the wrong
COCOS in its header; the residual step shows what a file-level inconsistency
looks like.
:::

## Session workflow

representation $\rightarrow$ shape $\rightarrow$ analytic equilibrium and scans

$\rightarrow$ EFIT of one discharge $\rightarrow$ its validation $\rightarrow$ coordinates

$\rightarrow$ kinetic EFIT $\rightarrow$ derived state $\rightarrow$ residual and CHEASE $\rightarrow$ times and shots

::: {.notes}
[1 min]

NARRATE:
Point at each step. Note that "coordinates" is a real step, not bookkeeping: a
profile without its radial coordinate is not a physics claim. The real
equilibrium is shown *before* its constraints are read: students first see the
state, then ask whether the measurements and weights support it. Each step ends
with a short "Check yourself".
:::

## What kinetic data changes

Magnetic EFIT $\rightarrow$ kinetic EFIT: $\beta_p$, $\beta_N$ roughly double;
$q$ and $\ell_i$ stay put.

A magnetics-only $\beta$ is not a measured pressure.

::: {.notes}
[3 min]

NARRATE:
Same instant of 48224, same magnetics, plus Thomson pressure points. The
magnetics fix the boundary and the current profile; the pressure was nearly
free. Put it beside the $\nu$ scan: the model says pressure matters, the
experiment says how much of it the magnetics could identify. Sensitivity and
identifiability are different questions.

Then close the loop: the Grad--Shafranov residual of both files is about one
percent, and CHEASE's `EquilibriumVariation` perturbs the reconstructed
equilibrium on purpose --- `current_peaking` is how $\ell_i$ moves, never a
uniform $FF'$ scale.
:::
